issues.description: The Latin has no plural referent: 'separat mare eum, qui fecerat mare' = 'the sea does not separate him, who had made the sea.' 'eum' is the accusative direct object of 'separat' and is the same person as 'qui fecerat mare' (the Maker of the sea). The translation invents an unstated object 'them' and demotes 'him who had made the sea' to the object of 'from', changing who is said to be separated from whom.

issues.span: does not separate them from him who had made the sea
issues.description: The faithful reading is 'the sea does not separate him who had made the sea' (the Maker of the sea is not cut off by his own sea). The English recasts the direct object 'eum ... qui fecerat mare' as an oblique reference point, reversing the grammatical relationship the Latin states.

issues.span: who lived in the same age as Pudens
issues.description: The Latin reads 'quae eodem cum illo vixit seculo' — 'who lived in the same age with him/that one.' 'illo' is a masculine pronoun whose natural antecedent in the sentence is Plutarch (is / Plutarchum), and the rhetorical point is precisely that this Claudia was Plutarch's own contemporary (unlike the 'prisca' Vestal). The translation resolves the bare pronoun to the proper name 'Pudens,' which appears nowhere in the Latin and most likely misidentifies the referent, distorting the argument.
The emphatic particle 'utique' in 'Vestalis utique illius nominatissimae' ('that most celebrated Vestal, assuredly/indeed') is dropped; non-critical, but the emphasis is lost.
The Latin 'Vestalis utique illius nominatissimae' includes 'utique' (certainly / at any rate / especially), an intensifying particle that is dropped in the English.

'cum ... faciat' (cum + subjunctive) here is causal/adversative ('since/whereas he makes mention'), carrying the logical contrast of the argument; rendering it as temporal 'when' weakens the intended 'since/whereas' sense.

Latin 'circa quamuis rem' = 'about any thing whatsoever'; the universalizing force of 'quamuis' (any thing at all) is softened to the vaguer 'some object', losing the nuance that the excessive zeal may attach to anything.
Latin 'hominem ... trahit' is singular ('drags the man'); rendered as plural 'men'. Low impact as a generic statement, but the number does not match the Latin.

Latin 'atque adeo perfectissimi' means 'and indeed (even) the most perfect'; 'adeo' here is an intensifier ('and what is more/and indeed'), not a restrictive 'only'. Rendering it as 'only' adds a restrictive nuance not strictly in the Latin, though it is a defensible reading given 'pauci'.

Latin 'furorem ... percipiunt' means the few/most perfect 'perceive, apprehend, or experience' this frenzy (percipere = to grasp/take in). 'achieve' shifts the sense toward attaining or reaching the state rather than apprehending it; meaning is largely preserved but slightly altered.
Latin 'modum' (measure/limit) is rendered 'a proper limit'; 'proper' is a slight amplification, though defensible since 'modus' connotes due measure.

Latin 'diuini furoris' renders the Platonic technical term (theia mania, Phaedrus 265a-b) for divine inspiration/madness/frenzy. In this context 'furor' means divine frenzy/madness, not 'rage,' which misleadingly connotes anger rather than inspired possession.

issues.span: the gathering of all the good men, the faces and expressions of all these
issues.description: The entire fifth member of the Latin enumeration, 'hic munitissimus habendi senatus locus' ('this most fortified place for holding the senate'), is dropped. The English jumps from 'concursus bonorum omnium' straight to 'horum ora voltusque', omitting one of the six parallel 'nihil...' clauses.

issues.span: the faces and expressions of all these people
issues.description: The Latin 'horum ora voltusque' is 'the faces and countenances of these (men)'; 'all' has no counterpart here ('omnium' modifies only 'bonorum' earlier in the sentence), so 'all these people' slightly over-renders 'horum'. Meaning preserved; non-critical.
The Latin reads 'Demosthenes philosophus' (Demosthenes the philosopher). 'philosophus' means philosopher, not 'orator'; this misidentifies the figure's designation as given in the source.

issues.span: Apollo over the third; and the Muses over the fourth
issues.description: The Latin assigns 'tertio musas' (the Muses to the third frenzy) and 'quarto apollinem' (Apollo to the fourth). The translation reverses them, giving Apollo the third and the Muses the fourth.
